newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish strike nears end but protests continue.
newsitem.headline: Spanish strike nears end but protests continue.

text.p: Strike pickets stepped up their protest actions along Spanish highways on Wednesday as talks to end a two-week truckers' strike ended a marathon overnight session on a positive note, officials said.
Negotiators expressed cautious optimism that the strike could be called off sometime during the day, but pickets stepped up their protests, firebombing trucks and attacking drivers.

Jose Luis Soldevilla, spokesman for the striking truckers, said he was "hopeful the happy news could be announced today" as he presented a new offer on early retirement, the sticking point in talks with the government.

During a break near midnight in the 15-hour session the day before, Soldevilla had told journalists a solution appeared "feasible" to the government's refusal to fund the truckers' demand for retirement at age 60 instead of 65.

Both sides in the negotiations, which Soldevilla described as "tense", have agreed to keep quiet on the contents of the talks but there were hints that it was in a final phase, notably the optimism shown by truckers in various regions.

Transporters in the central province of Burgos and on the Balearic Islands called off work stoppages, saying there had been progress. Taxi drivers, who are seeking the same kind of benefits as the truckers, decided to stop protest action pending talks.
Analysts in Spain also expected a solution soon, based on government concessions.

"It does look like they will give in at least part of the way (to strikers' demands) and unfortunately this could have a trickle-down effect to other sectors," Heinrick Lumholdt, chief economist for Bank of America in Madrid, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

Petrol station owners threatened on Tuesday to stop pumping indefinitely if the government did not reconsider a planned liberalisation of the sector, which would allow truckers to buy fuel directly from wholesalers and bypass the filling stations.
This would cut back petrol stations' profit margins.
Carmakers struggled on Wednesday to restart production after police escorts helped unblock roads.

Volkswagen subsidiary SEAT began production at its Martorell plant after a two-day stoppage, but the German carmaker halted production of its Polo model at its main plant in Wolfsburg, Germany, which uses Spanish-made parts.
